title: Onset, severity and course words
blurb: Define the words for how an illness starts, flares, fades, returns and ends, and avoid the paired-opposite traps.
question: “The disease had an insidious onset and a progressive course, with no period of remission.” Would you mark insidious as “sudden”? Most test takers do. What do these three words really say about the patient?

teach.h: Words that tell an illness's story
teach.body: Onset and course words describe the life of an illness: how it begins (acute, insidious, abrupt), how long it lasts (chronic, transient), how it changes (exacerbation, remission, relapse, progressive) and how it ends (benign, malignant, terminal). Formally, they describe the onset, duration, severity and outcome of a disease. Plain English: they answer when it started, how fast, how long, and how it will turn out.

teach.h: Three shapes of illness over time
teach.caption: Acute spikes fast and fades. Chronic lasts. Insidious creeps in unnoticed; progressive keeps climbing.

teach.h: Flare and fade: the course words
teach.caption: To exacerbate is to make worse; to recur is to happen again. The cycle can repeat.

head: Word
Meaning
Paired with
teach.caption: Morbidity is illness (or the disease rate); mortality is death (or the death rate).

teach.h: Where it comes from, where it goes
Scenario: Daniel reads a clinic summary
teach.body: Daniel, a respiratory therapy applicant, reads a summary for a patient named Mrs. Ward: “Chronic lung disease with an acute exacerbation last week. Symptoms are now intermittent. Prognosis is good if she avoids smoke, which exacerbates her condition. No complications.” He wants to explain the summary to a classmate in plain words.

items: Chronic: the lung disease is long-lasting.
Acute exacerbation: a sudden flare-up made it worse last week.
Intermittent: the symptoms now come and go instead of staying constant.
Prognosis is good: the expected outcome is favorable. Exacerbates: smoke makes it worse.
No complications: no new problems arose during the illness.

teach.text: Insidious is not “sudden.” It means so gradual that the illness is established before anyone notices. Latent is not “late”: it means present but inactive. Congenital is not “inherited”: it means present at birth. And imminent (about to happen) is not eminent (famous). Each trap is a word that looks or sounds right.

items: Acute = sudden and short; chronic = long or recurring; insidious = gradual and unnoticed; transient = brief.
Exacerbation (flare) vs remission (fading) vs relapse (return); recur = happen again.
Benign vs malignant; diagnosis (what it is) vs prognosis (how it will turn out).
Congenital = present at birth; hereditary = passed through genes; idiopathic = unknown cause.
Systemic = whole body; localized = one area; latent = present but inactive.

summary: You can now define the words that describe an illness's onset, duration, course and outcome. You can also reject the paired traps: acute and chronic, remission and relapse, diagnosis and prognosis, congenital and hereditary, imminent and eminent.

A.q: Mr. Grant's chronic back pain makes long drives difficult, so he stops every hour to stretch. What is the best definition of the word “chronic” in this sentence?
A.why: Chronic means lasting a long time or recurring often.

whyNot.0: Sudden and severe describes acute, the opposite.
whyNot.2: Sharp describes the quality of pain, not how long it lasts.
whyNot.3: Mild and passing describes a transient problem.

A.q: Pollen season triggered an exacerbation of Tia's asthma, and she used her rescue inhaler twice that day. What is the best definition of the word “exacerbation” in this sentence?
A.why: An exacerbation is a flare-up: a period when a disease worsens.

whyNot.1: A recovery is closer to remission, the opposite.
whyNot.2: An exaggeration is an overstatement, a look-alike word.
whyNot.3: A diagnosis identifies a disease; it does not worsen it.

A.q: Dr. Ward told Mr. Cole that the mole on his back was benign and could stay. What is the best definition of the word “benign” in this sentence?
A.why: Benign means not harmful; in medicine, not cancerous.

whyNot.3: A new mole can still be benign; the word describes harm, not age.

B.q: Type 2 diabetes can be insidious, so adults are often screened even when they feel well. What is the best definition of the word “insidious” in this sentence?
B.why: Insidious means developing so gradually that it is well established before it is noticed.

whyNot.0: Sudden and severe is acute, the opposite.
whyNot.2: Rare describes how common a disease is, not how it develops.

B.q: The chickenpox virus can remain latent in nerve cells for years before it causes shingles. What is the best definition of the word “latent” in this sentence?
B.why: Latent means present but not yet active, visible or causing symptoms.

whyNot.1: Latent looks like late, but it means dormant, not delayed.

B.q: Because the cancer was found early, the oncologist gave Mrs. Diaz a hopeful prognosis. What is the best definition of the word “prognosis” in this sentence?
B.why: A prognosis is the expected course or outcome of a disease.

whyNot.0: Identifying the disease is the diagnosis.
whyNot.2: A treatment schedule is a regimen.
whyNot.3: A referral sends the patient to another provider; it predicts nothing.

C.q: Which word describes a condition that is present at birth, whether or not it was inherited?
C.why: Congenital means present at birth. Some congenital conditions are inherited and some are not.

whyNot.0: Hereditary means passed down through genes, which may show up later in life.
whyNot.2: Chronic describes duration, not timing at birth.

C.q: With the hurricane's landfall imminent, the hospital moved patients away from the windows. What is the best definition of the word “imminent” in this sentence?
C.why: Imminent means about to happen very soon.

whyNot.0: Widely respected is eminent, the classic sound-alike.
whyNot.1: Recently ended is the opposite of approaching.
whyNot.2: A hurricane may be feared, but imminent describes timing.

C.q: The specialist classified Ms. Fox's lung scarring as idiopathic after reviewing years of records. What is the best definition of the word “idiopathic” in this sentence?
C.why: Idiopathic means arising from an unknown cause.

reteach.title: An illness is like a storm forecast
reteach.question: A weather forecaster says a storm will come on suddenly, linger, ease off, then return. Couldn't a nurse describe an illness the same way?

blocks.body: A flash thunderstorm is acute: it hits fast and is over soon. A long drought is chronic. Fog that thickens so slowly you only notice when you cannot see the road is insidious. A storm that strengthens is an exacerbation; a break in the clouds is remission; the rain returning is relapse. The forecast itself, what will probably happen, is the prognosis.

blocks.text: The forecast (prognosis) predicts; naming today's weather is the diagnosis. Do not swap them.

explain.body: Acute means sudden and short; chronic means long-lasting or recurring; insidious means so gradual it goes unnoticed; transient means brief and passing; abrupt means sudden and unexpected.

test.q: Mr. Hall's acute kidney injury followed a severe bout of food poisoning last weekend. What is the best definition of the word “acute” in this sentence?
test.why: In onset language, acute means coming on suddenly and running a short course.

whyNot.3: Without symptoms describes a latent or silent condition.

explain.body: An exacerbation is a flare-up; remission is a lessening of signs; relapse is a return; intermittent means stopping and starting; progressive means getting steadily worse; recur means to happen again.

test.q: Lisa's intermittent headaches make it hard for her to plan a regular study schedule. What is the best definition of the word “intermittent” in this sentence?
test.why: Intermittent means starting and stopping at intervals; not continuous.

explain.body: Benign means not cancerous; malignant means cancerous; terminal means leading to death; fatal means causing death. A diagnosis names the disease, and a prognosis predicts its outcome.

test.q: The hospice nurse visits patients with terminal illnesses and supports their families at home. What is the best definition of the word “terminal” in this sentence?
test.why: In a medical sentence, terminal means leading to death; in the final stage.

whyNot.1: Long-lasting is chronic; a chronic illness need not be fatal.
whyNot.2: Recently diagnosed describes timing of diagnosis, not the outcome.

explain.body: Congenital means present at birth; hereditary means passed down through genes; idiopathic means of unknown cause; systemic means affecting the whole body; localized means confined to one area.

test.q: The infection stayed localized to the cut on Ben's thumb, so the doctor did not prescribe pills. What is the best definition of the word “localized” in this sentence?
test.why: Localized means confined to one area.

whyNot.0: Affecting the whole body is systemic, the opposite.
whyNot.1: Caused by a virus is viral.
whyNot.3: A localized infection may heal quickly or slowly; the word describes location.
